1:3.t: "Since I myself have carefully investigated everything from the very beginning": the KJV's "having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first". "Theophilus" means "friend of God"; "most excellent" suggests an official of rank.

1:5.t: Names follow their Old Testament spelling: Zechariah for the KJV's "Zacharias", Abijah for "Abia", Elizabeth for "Elisabeth". The priests were divided into twenty-four divisions that served in turn (1 Chronicles 24:10).

1:9.t: There were so many priests that one might offer incense only once in a lifetime.

1:15.t: "Even before he is born": the KJV's "even from his mother's womb".

1:26.t: "In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy": the KJV's "in the sixth month"; see 1:24, 1:36.

1:27.t: "Pledged to be married": the KJV's "espoused". See Matthew 1:18.

1:28.t: "Blessed are you among women": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here (compare 1:42).
"Highly favored" (Greek kecharitomene, from charis, grace): "one who has been graced". The favor is God's free gift to Mary, not a reward she earned.

1:34.t: "Since I am a virgin": the KJV's "seeing I know not a man".

1:36.t: "Relative": the KJV's "cousin", which in 1611 meant any kinsperson.

1:63.t: "Writing tablet": the KJV's "writing table", a board coated with wax.

1:69.t: "A horn of salvation": the horn is a symbol of strength (Psalm 18:2, 132:17).

1:80.t: "Until he appeared publicly to Israel": the KJV's "till the day of his shewing unto Israel".

2:1.t: "A census ... of the entire Roman world": the KJV's "that all the world should be taxed". The census registered people for taxation.

2:2.t: "Quirinius": the KJV's "Cyrenius", the Greek spelling. A census under Quirinius is known from AD 6; the Greek may also mean "before Quirinius was governor".

2:7.t: "Cloths": the KJV's "swaddling clothes", strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn. "The inn": the Greek kataluma may mean a guest room in a family home (compare 22:11).

2:14.t: "Good will toward people": the KJV's reading. Many early manuscripts read "peace among those on whom His favor rests".
"Peace" (Greek eirene, Hebrew shalom): not only the absence of conflict but wholeness and well-being given by God.

2:24.t: "Doves": the KJV's "turtledoves". A pair of birds was the offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8).

2:25.t: "The consolation of Israel": the coming of the Messiah to comfort His people (Isaiah 40:1).

2:33.t: "The child's father and mother": the KJV's "Joseph and his mother"; many early manuscripts read "His father and mother".

2:36.t: "Penuel": the KJV's "Phanuel". "Asher": the KJV's "Aser". "Until she was eighty-four": the Greek may also mean "for eighty-four years", the KJV's reading "a widow of about fourscore and four years" allowing either.

3:1.t: The fifteenth year of Tiberius was about AD 28-29. "Iturea and Traconitis" were regions northeast of Galilee.

3:2.t: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office from AD 18 to 36, but Annas kept great influence.

3:22.t: "You are My Son, whom I love": the KJV's "Thou art my beloved Son".

3:23.t: Names with Old Testament equivalents follow their Old Testament spelling (Zerubbabel, Shealtiel, Nahshon, Terah, Methuselah, Mahalalel, Kenan, Enosh); the others keep the Greek forms. Luke's list differs from Matthew's between David and Joseph. Many think Luke gives Mary's line through her father Heli, or Joseph's legal line through an adoption or levirate marriage.

3:36.t: "Cainan" is not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, but appears in the Greek Old Testament.

4:4.t: "But on every word of God": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words. The quotation is Deuteronomy 8:3.

4:5.t: "To a high place": the KJV's "into an high mountain"; many early manuscripts do not have "mountain".

4:8.t: "Get behind Me, Satan! For": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here (compare Matthew 4:10). The quotation is Deuteronomy 6:13.

4:10.t: Quotations of Psalm 91:11-12 and Deuteronomy 6:16. Luke gives the temptations in a different order from Matthew, ending at the temple in Jerusalem.

4:18.t: A quotation of Isaiah 61:1-2, with 58:6. "To heal the brokenhearted": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.
"Anointed" (Greek chrio): the verb from which christos, "Christ", comes. Jesus announces Himself as the Spirit-anointed One of Isaiah 61.

4:25.t: See 1 Kings 17:8-24 and 2 Kings 5:1-14. "Zarephath": the KJV's "Sarepta". "Elisha": the KJV's "Eliseus".

4:44.t: "Galilee": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Judea", meaning the land of the Jews in general.

5:1.t: The Lake of Gennesaret is the Sea of Galilee.

5:19.t: "Through the tiles": the KJV's "through the tiling".

5:20.t: "Friend": the KJV's "Man", a polite form of address.

5:39.t: "Better": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "good".

6:1.t: "On the second Sabbath after the first": the KJV's reading, of uncertain meaning; many early manuscripts read simply "on a Sabbath".

6:16.t: "Judas the brother of James": the KJV's reading. The Greek says only "Judas of James", which usually means "son of James". He is Thaddaeus in Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18.

6:17.t: "A level place": the KJV's "the plain". Luke's sermon parallels Matthew 5-7.

6:29.t: "Coat ... shirt": the KJV's "cloke ... coat". See Matthew 5:40.

6:38.t: "Into your lap": the KJV's "into your bosom", the fold of a robe above the belt, used as a pocket.

7:2.t: "Whom his master valued highly": the KJV's "who was dear unto him".

7:11.t: Nain was a village about ten kilometers southeast of Nazareth.

7:14.t: "Bier": an open frame on which the body was carried to burial.

7:30.t: "The experts in the law": the KJV's "lawyers".

7:41.t: "Five hundred denarii ... fifty": the KJV's "five hundred pence ... fifty". A denarius was a day's wage.

7:44.t: Washing a guest's feet, a kiss of greeting and anointing the head with oil were customary courtesies.

8:3.t: "Chuza, the manager of Herod's household": the KJV's "Chuza Herod's steward". "Support Him": the KJV's reading; many manuscripts read "them", Jesus and the Twelve.

8:26.t: "Gadarenes": the KJV's reading; many manuscripts read "Gerasenes" or "Gergesenes". Also 8:37.

8:31.t: "The Abyss": the KJV's "the deep", the place of imprisonment for evil spirits (Revelation 9:1-2, 20:1-3).

8:43.t: "She had spent all she had on doctors": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

9:10.t: Bethsaida was on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, near where the Jordan enters it.

9:54.t: "As Elijah did": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words. See 2 Kings 1:10-12.

9:55.t: "And said, 'You do not know what kind of spirit you are of. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives, but to save them'": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

10:1.t: "Seventy": the KJV's reading; many manuscripts read "seventy-two". Also 10:17. The number may recall the seventy nations of Genesis 10.

10:4.t: "Do not greet anyone on the road": Eastern greetings could be long and elaborate; the mission was urgent.

10:6.t: "Someone who promotes peace": the KJV's "the son of peace", a Hebrew idiom for a person of peace.

10:30.t: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho dropped about a thousand meters in about 27 kilometers through desert, notorious for robbers.

10:33.t: Jews and Samaritans had been bitter enemies for centuries (John 4:9).

10:35.t: "Two denarii": the KJV's "two pence", two days' wages.

11:2.t: "In heaven ... Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven ... but deliver us from evil": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts have the shorter form "Father, may Your name be kept holy. Your kingdom come ... And lead us not into temptation."

11:11.t: "Bread ... a stone": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have this first pair here (compare Matthew 7:9).

11:44.t: Walking over a grave made a person ceremonially unclean (Numbers 19:16). The Pharisees defile those around them without their knowing.

12:6.t: "Two pennies": the KJV's "two farthings"; Greek assarion. See Matthew 10:29.

12:25.t: "About half a meter": the KJV's "one cubit". See Matthew 6:27.

12:38.t: "The second or third watch of the night": from about nine at night to three in the morning, by the Jewish reckoning of three watches.

13:1.t: This massacre is not recorded elsewhere; Pilate was known for such brutality.

13:4.t: Siloam was a district in southern Jerusalem, near the pool of that name.

13:21.t: "About 22 liters of flour": the KJV's "three measures of meal". See Matthew 13:33.

13:32.t: "That fox": Herod Antipas. "I will reach My goal": the KJV's "I shall be perfected"; the Greek teleioumai means to finish or complete.

13:35.t: A quotation of Psalm 118:26. "Desolate": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have this word.

14:2.t: "Dropsy": swelling caused by fluid in the body, now called edema.

14:5.t: "A donkey or an ox": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "a son or an ox".

14:10.t: "You will be honored": the KJV's "then shalt thou have worship", "worship" meaning honor in 1611.

15:8.t: "Ten silver coins": the KJV's "ten pieces of silver"; Greek drachme, a Greek coin worth about a day's wage, like the denarius.

15:16.t: "Pods": the KJV's "husks", carob pods used as animal feed.

15:22.t: The robe, ring and sandals marked him as a son, not a servant.

16:1.t: "Manager": the KJV's "steward", a man who ran his master's business.

16:6.t: "About 2,200 liters of olive oil ... 1,100": the KJV's "an hundred measures of oil ... fifty"; Greek batos, the Hebrew bath, about 22 liters.

16:7.t: "About 22,000 liters of wheat ... 17,600": the KJV's "an hundred measures of wheat ... fourscore"; Greek koros, the Hebrew kor or homer, about 220 liters.

16:9.t: "Worldly wealth": the KJV's "the mammon of unrighteousness". "When it is gone": the KJV's "when ye fail"; many early manuscripts read "when it fails".

16:17.t: "The least stroke of a pen": the KJV's "one tittle". See Matthew 5:18.

16:22.t: "Abraham's side": the KJV's "Abraham's bosom", the place of honor beside the host at a feast, a picture of blessing after death.

17:6.t: "Mulberry tree": the KJV's "sycamine tree", the black mulberry, known for its deep roots.

17:12.t: People with leprosy had to keep their distance from others (Leviticus 13:45-46).

17:36.t: Some early manuscripts do not have this verse (compare Matthew 24:40).

18:12.t: The law required only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29-31).

19:2.t: A chief tax collector oversaw other collectors. Jericho was a center of trade.

19:4.t: "Sycamore-fig": the KJV's "sycomore", a fig tree with low, spreading branches, not the American sycamore.

19:8.t: The law required a fourfold repayment only for stolen livestock (Exodus 22:1); Zacchaeus goes beyond what was required.

19:12.t: Herod's son Archelaus had gone to Rome to be confirmed as king in 4 BC, and a Jewish delegation followed to oppose him.

19:13.t: "Ten minas": the KJV's "ten pounds". A mina was a sum of money worth about a hundred denarii, or about four months' wages.

20:16.t: "May this never happen!": the KJV's "God forbid", the Greek me genoito.

21:8.t: "And the time is near": the KJV punctuates this as Jesus' own warning; many modern Bibles take it as the claim of the false teachers.

21:20.t: Roman armies besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

22:4.t: "The officers of the temple guard": the KJV's "captains", Levites who kept order in the temple.

22:14.t: "Reclined at the table": the KJV's "sat down". See Matthew 26:7.

22:19.t: "Given for you ... poured out for you": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts end the verse at "This is My body" and do not have verse 20.

"In remembrance" (Greek anamnesis): more than recalling a past event; at Passover Israel retold the Exodus as their own story. The Lord's Supper makes Jesus' saving death present to those who share it.

22:25.t: "Benefactors": a title kings and patrons took for themselves.

22:43.t: The KJV includes these verses; some early manuscripts do not have them.

22:44.t: "Like drops of blood": the KJV's "as it were great drops of blood". Luke compares His sweat to drops of blood; under extreme stress, blood can mix with sweat.

23:5.t: "All over Judea": the KJV's "throughout all Jewry", the land of the Jews.

23:17.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it.

23:31.t: "When the tree is green ... when it is dry": if the Romans treat the innocent this way, how much worse will it be for the guilty?

23:33.t: "Calvary": the KJV's name, from the Latin calvaria, "skull"; the Greek kranion, Aramaic Golgotha.

23:34.t: "Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing'": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

23:38.t: "In letters of Greek, Latin and Hebrew": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here (compare John 19:20).

23:44.t: "About noon ... three in the afternoon": the KJV's "about the sixth hour ... the ninth hour". "Land": the Greek ge can mean "land" or "earth"; the KJV has "earth".

23:45.t: "The sun was darkened": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the sun's light failed".

24:12.t: Some early manuscripts do not have this verse.

24:13.t: "About eleven kilometers": the KJV's "about threescore furlongs", sixty stadia.

24:42.t: "And some honeycomb": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

24:51.t: "And was taken up into heaven": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words. Luke tells of the ascension in more detail in Acts 1:9-11.

1:35.t: "Overshadow" (Greek episkiazo): the word used of the cloud of God's presence over the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35, Greek) and at the transfiguration (9:34).

1:37.t: "No word from God will ever fail" (Greek ouk adynatesei para tou theou pan rhema): the KJV's "with God nothing shall be impossible". Rhema means both "word" and "thing", so both readings are possible. The angel echoes Genesis 18:14.

1:46.t: Mary's song, called the Magnificat from its first word in Latin. It echoes Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1-10) and many psalms. "Mercy" (Greek eleos) in verses 50, 54 and 72 stands for the Hebrew hesed, God's steadfast love and covenant loyalty.

1:47.t: "God my Savior" (Greek soter): Mary calls God her Savior, as He is called throughout the Old Testament (Psalm 106:21, Isaiah 45:21).

1:68.t: Zechariah's song, called the Benedictus from its first word in Latin.

1:78.t: "The rising sun from on high" (Greek anatole): the KJV's "the dayspring". Anatole means sunrise but also translates the Hebrew tsemach, "Branch", in the Greek Old Testament (Jeremiah 23:5, Zechariah 3:8, 6:12). It points to the Messiah. Compare Malachi 4:2.

2:11.t: "Savior ... Christ the Lord" (Greek soter, christos kyrios): three titles together. "Savior" and "Lord" were also claimed by the Roman emperor; the angel gives them to a baby in a feeding trough.

2:29.t: Simeon's song, called the Nunc Dimittis from its first words in Latin. "Dismiss" (Greek apolyo) was used for releasing a slave from duty.

2:49.t: "About My Father's business": the KJV's reading. The Greek en tois tou patros mou means literally "in the things of My Father" and can also mean "in My Father's house". Both fit: Jesus is in the temple, doing His Father's work.

4:19.t: "The year of the Lord's favor" (Greek eniauton kyriou dekton): the KJV's "the acceptable year of the Lord", recalling the Year of Jubilee, when debts were canceled and slaves freed (Leviticus 25:10). Jesus stops before "the day of vengeance of our God" (Isaiah 61:2).

4:21.t: "Today" (Greek semeron): a key word in Luke (2:11, 19:9, 23:43). In Jesus the promised salvation is present now.

5:8.t: "I am a sinful man": in the presence of holiness Peter sees himself truly, as Isaiah did (Isaiah 6:5).

5:10.t: "You will fish for people" (Greek anthropous ese zogron): the KJV's "thou shalt catch men". Zogreo means "to catch alive".

6:20.t: "Blessed" (Greek makarios): see Matthew 5:3. Luke's version speaks directly to "you who are poor" and adds woes (6:24-26).

6:36.t: "Merciful" (Greek oiktirmon): full of compassion. Matthew 5:48 has "perfect"; Luke shows that God's perfection is His mercy.

7:13.t: "His heart went out to her" (Greek esplanchnisthe): the KJV's "he had compassion". See Matthew 9:36.

7:16.t: "God has come to help His people" (Greek epeskepsato): the KJV's "God hath visited his people", the same word Zechariah used (1:68, 1:78). In the Old Testament God "visits" to save or to judge.

7:47.t: "Her many sins have been forgiven, for she loved much": her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its cause, as the parable shows (7:41-43) and Jesus says in 7:50: "Your faith has saved you."

8:15.t: "Persevering" (Greek hypomone): the KJV's "patience", steady endurance under pressure.

9:23.t: "Daily" (Greek kath hemeran): Luke alone adds this word. Following Jesus means dying to self every day, not only in a single act.

9:31.t: "Departure" (Greek exodos): the KJV's "decease". Jesus' death, resurrection and ascension will be a new Exodus, delivering God's people as He once led Israel out of Egypt.

9:51.t: "Resolutely set out" (Greek to prosopon esterisen): literally "set His face", a Hebrew idiom for firm determination (Isaiah 50:7). From here Luke's Gospel follows Jesus' journey to Jerusalem and the cross. "Taken up" (Greek analempsis) refers to His ascension (Acts 1:2).

10:29.t: "Justify himself" (Greek dikaiosai heauton): to prove himself right. The parable turns his question around: not "Who is my neighbor?" but "Who acted as a neighbor?"

10:37.t: "Had mercy" (Greek eleos): the Hebrew idea of hesed in action, faithful love that does what is needed (compare Micah 6:8).

10:41.t: "Worried" (Greek merimnao): see Matthew 6:25. "Only one thing is needed": the KJV's reading. Some early manuscripts read "few things are needed, or only one".

11:8.t: "Shameless audacity" (Greek anaideia): the KJV's "importunity". The word means shamelessness, boldness that does not give up.

11:20.t: "The finger of God": recalls Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh's magicians admitted God's power. Matthew 12:28 has "the Spirit of God".

12:15.t: "Greed" (Greek pleonexia): the KJV's "covetousness", the craving for more.

12:19.t: "Myself ... your life" (Greek psyche): the KJV's "my soul ... thy soul". The rich man speaks to his own soul as though possessions could satisfy it.

12:50.t: "Baptism": Jesus speaks of His coming death as a baptism, an overwhelming flood He must pass through (compare Mark 10:38).

13:3.t: "Repent": see Matthew 3:2. Jesus refuses to treat disaster as a measure of someone's guilt; instead He calls every hearer to repent.

13:5.t: "Repent": see Matthew 3:2. Jesus refuses to treat disaster as a measure of someone's guilt; instead He calls every hearer to repent.

13:24.t: "Make every effort" (Greek agonizesthe): the KJV's "strive", from the word for an athletic contest.

14:26.t: "Hate" (Greek miseo): a Semitic way of saying "love less by comparison" (compare Genesis 29:30-31, Matthew 10:37). Jesus demands first place, above even family, not literal hatred.

15:7.t: "Repents" (Greek metanoeo): see Matthew 3:2. All three parables end in joy when the lost is found.

15:10.t: "Repents" (Greek metanoeo): see Matthew 3:2. All three parables end in joy when the lost is found.

15:20.t: "Filled with compassion" (Greek splanchnizomai): see Matthew 9:36. A dignified older man did not run; the father's running shows the depth of his love.

16:8.t: "Shrewdly" (Greek phronimos): wisely, prudently. The master praises the manager's foresight, not his dishonesty. Jesus urges His followers to use money with the same foresight for eternal ends.

16:23.t: "Hades": the KJV's "hell". Hades is the realm of the dead (see Matthew 11:23). In this parable it is a place of torment for the rich man, separated from the comfort of the righteous.

17:10.t: "Unworthy" (Greek achreios): the KJV's "unprofitable", meaning that servants who only do their duty have earned no special credit.

17:19.t: "Made you well" (Greek sozo): see Matthew 9:22. All ten were cleansed, but the Samaritan who returned to give thanks was told he was made whole.

17:21.t: "Within you" (Greek entos hymon): the KJV's reading. Entos can mean "within" or "among". Jesus was speaking to Pharisees, and many take it to mean "the kingdom of God is in your midst", present in Him.

18:13.t: "Have mercy on me" (Greek hilastheti moi): literally "be propitiated toward me", "be reconciled to me". The verb is related to the mercy seat, where atonement was made (Hebrews 9:5).

18:14.t: "Justified" (Greek dedikaiomenos): declared righteous by God. See Matthew 12:37. The one who trusted God's mercy, not his own record, went home right with God.

19:10.t: "To seek and to save the lost": the theme verse of Luke's Gospel. Jesus is the Shepherd of Ezekiel 34:16.

19:42.t: "What would bring you peace": in Hebrew, Jerusalem's name was heard as containing shalom, "peace" (Hebrews 7:2).

19:44.t: "The time of God's coming to you" (Greek ton kairon tes episkopes sou): the KJV's "the time of thy visitation". See 1:68 and 7:16.

20:36.t: "Children of the resurrection" (Greek huioi tes anastaseos): a Hebrew idiom meaning those who share in the resurrection.

20:38.t: "To Him all are alive": those who have died are not lost to God. He remains their God, so they will rise.

22:15.t: "I have eagerly desired" (Greek epithymia epethymesa): literally "with desire I have desired", a Hebrew way of saying "I have longed with all My heart".

22:20.t: "The new covenant" (Greek he kaine diatheke): see Matthew 26:28 and Jeremiah 31:31-34.

22:31.t: "All of you ... you, Simon": in verse 31 "you" is plural (all the disciples); in verse 32 it is singular (Peter). "Turned back" (Greek epistrepsas): the KJV's "converted", returned to faith after his denial.

22:36.t: "Sell your cloak and buy one": a vivid way of saying that hard times are coming. When the disciples take Him literally, He says "That is enough!" (22:38), and He stops them from using a sword (22:51).

22:70.t: "You say that I am" (Greek hymeis legete hoti ego eimi): a guarded yes, as in Matthew 26:64. They took it as a full admission.

23:43.t: "Paradise" (Greek paradeisos, from a Persian word for a walled garden): used in the Greek Old Testament for the garden of Eden. In Jesus' day it meant the place of blessing for the righteous after death (2 Corinthians 12:4, Revelation 2:7).

23:46.t: "Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit": a quotation of Psalm 31:5, a prayer Jewish children were taught to say at bedtime. Jesus adds "Father".

24:26.t: "Have to" (Greek dei): "it was necessary". Luke uses this word to show that Jesus' suffering was part of God's plan (9:22, 17:25, 22:37, 24:7, 24:44).

24:27.t: "Moses and all the Prophets ... the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms": the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible. Jesus teaches that the whole Old Testament points to Him.

24:44.t: "Moses and all the Prophets ... the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms": the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible. Jesus teaches that the whole Old Testament points to Him.

24:49.t: "What My Father has promised": the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost (Acts 1:4-5, 2:1-4).
